To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) spikes are generated only when the amplitude of an EPSG exceeds the neuron’s expectation (“prediction error”), 2) excitability is an accurate prediction of the amplitude of an incoming EPSG, and 3) the diversity of synaptic inputs, voltage-regulated ion currents, and other mechanisms implements “predictive homeostatasis” to maintain accurate predictions.
the neuron’s membrane excitatory conductance is an expectation, and that the neuron generates a spike when the actual value of this conductance exceeds its expectation.
the probability of a spike is the probability of a prediction error and that a neuron’s excitability is an optimal estimate of the mean amplitude of future excitatory postsnaptic conductances.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding why neurons fire action potentials, how they achieve this, and how they control the probability that they will spike.
the question: What is the meaning of spikes from a neuron’s point of view?
the meaning of randomness, the role of homeostasis, the relationship between neural activity and synaptic vesicle release, and the relationship between neural coding and information theory.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the neuron’s spike output is “predictive” and “random” from the neuron’s own point of view, but “deterministic” from the external observer’s perspective.
“neurons are not random”.

spikes are random only from the point of view of external observers who are ignorant of the neuron’s inner workings, and that spikes would not appear random to a hypothetical observer with complete knowledge of the neuron’s inputs and internal state.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the meaning of a spike is to communicate the occurrence of prediction error.
the “random” nature of neural activity is a consequence of the neuron’s own ignorance, and that the “randomness” is a consequence of a homeostatic strategy for maintaining accurate predictions.
the meaning of randomness is in the eye of the beholder.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the conventional view of randomness in neural activity is incorrect and that spikes are not “random”, but rather they reflect a neuron’s predictions.
spikes are generated by prediction errors, not random fluctuations.
the conventional view of spikes as “random” is a misconception.
